name: Attribute substitution
statement: A proposed mechanism rather than a finding: asked a hard question, people are said to answer an easier one that comes to mind, and not to notice the swap.
meaning: Kahneman and Frederick proposed a single process behind the judgement heuristics. A judgement is mediated by a heuristic when a person assesses a target attribute by substituting a related heuristic attribute that comes more readily to mind. Representativeness becomes the use of similarity as the heuristic attribute for probability. Availability becomes the use of ease of retrieval, and affect becomes the use of liking. Kahneman set out three departures from the 1974 account of heuristics: a common substitution process, an extension beyond judgements about uncertain events, and an explicit treatment of when System 2 modifies or overrides the intuitive answer. Anchoring was excluded, because anchoring raises the accessibility of one value of the target attribute rather than swapping in a different attribute. The model carries two testable predictions. One group's judgement of the target attribute should track another group's judgement of the heuristic attribute. The person making the judgement should not notice that a different question has been answered.

origin.where: Heuristics and Biases: The Psychology of Intuitive Judgment
origin.note: Their chapter, "Representativeness Revisited: Attribute Substitution in Intuitive Judgment", occupies pages 49 to 81 of the volume edited by Gilovich, Griffin and Kahneman for Cambridge University Press. The chapter itself was not opened during this check. Its definition and its evidence are quoted here from Kahneman's restatement in American Psychologist the following year, which cites it.

evidence: Kahneman calls a categorical prediction study by Kahneman and Tversky the most direct evidence. Three groups saw the same nine fields of graduate specialisation. One estimated the relative frequency of students in each, giving means from 20% for humanities and education to 3% for library science. One ranked how far a description of a fictitious student, Tom W., resembled a typical student in each field. One ranked how likely Tom W. was to have specialised in each, having been told the sketch came from personality tests of dubious validity. The description was written to fit the smaller fields, and the correlation between representativeness rankings and estimated base rates was -0.62. Mean probability rankings correlated 0.98 with mean similarity rankings and -0.63 with base rates. The same design run on Linda produced the conjunction fallacy in both groups: 85% of the similarity group and 89% of the probability group put the conjunction item above its constituent. Tversky and Koehler had people rate the probability that the home team would win each of 20 basketball games and later rate the relative strength of the teams, and obtained a correlation of 0.99. In a survey by Strack, Martin and Schwarz the correlation between reported happiness and number of dates last month was negligible in that order and rose to 0.66 when the dating question came first. Every figure in this paragraph is read off Kahneman's 2003 article rather than the papers reporting the studies. The second line of evidence is the bat-and-ball problem. Frederick built it into the three-item Cognitive Reflection Test and gave that test to 3,428 respondents across 35 studies over 26 months from January 2003. The mean score was 1.24 out of 3, with 33% scoring zero and 17% scoring three, and location means ran from 2.18 at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology to 0.57 at the University of Toledo. De Neys, Rossi and Houdé supplied the substitution reading of the error: the relational clause "the bat costs $1 more than the ball" is read as the absolute "the bat costs $1".

replication.headline: The one substitution prediction with a direct replication behind it held at 264 people, while seven studies on the same problem found that most correct answers were never corrected at all.
replication.detail: De Neys, Rossi and Houdé tested whether people notice the swap. They gave 248 Caen undergraduates the standard problem and an isomorphic control that states the easier question outright, of the form "A magazine and a banana together cost $2.90. The magazine costs $2. How much does the banana cost?". Only 21% solved the standard problem, SE 2.3%, and 194 of the 195 errors were the "10 cents" answer. The control was solved by 98%, SE 1%, F(1, 247) = 714.94, p < .0001, partial eta-squared = .74. Reasoners who gave the substituted answer rated their confidence lower on the standard problem than on the control, F(1, 194) = 58.54, p < .0001, partial eta-squared = .23. Machalani, Gallant, Orha, Ostbo and Hehman repeated the design on 264 McGill undergraduates for the Collaborative Replications and Education Project. The confidence effect came out in the same direction, F(1, 114) = 31.62, p < .0001, with biased reasoners averaging 95.60% confidence on the control and 84.95% on the standard problem. The error rate did not repeat. Of the replication sample 97.72% solved the control, but 50.38% also solved the standard problem and 43.94% made the substituted error, where the original had 194 of its 248 participants giving it. What this design tests is awareness of the substitution rather than the substitution itself. Bago and De Neys ran seven studies in which people answered the bat-and-ball problem twice, first under a deadline and cognitive load and then after deliberation. Across the first five, 67.6% of correct final answers had already been given as the initial answer, and counting only each participant's first problem still gave 42%. On that evidence a correct answer usually does not follow the correction of a substituted one.

study.cite: Machalani, A., Gallant, A., Orha, V., Ostbo, N., & Hehman, E. (2020). Substitution sensitivity and the bat-and-ball problem: A direct replication of De Neys et al. (2013). McGill Science Undergraduate Research Journal, 15(1), 46-51.

limits: Attribute substitution is a mechanism rather than a result, so no study replicates it whole. Each test puts one prediction to one problem, and the two lines of evidence above are not tests of the same thing. No multi-site or multi-laboratory replication of any substitution test was located. Searches of Crossref, PubMed, the Open Science Framework and the Many Labs and Registered Replication Report catalogues turned up none. The heuristic elicitation studies, which Kahneman calls the most direct evidence, could not be checked against a replication here. A registered replication of Kahneman and Tversky's 1973 paper by Chan and Feldman holds Stage 1 acceptance at Peer Community in Registered Reports, and the page carrying its Stage 2 results refused automated requests during this check, so no figure from it appears on this page. The 2002 chapter and the 1973 paper were not opened either. Kahneman writes in the 2003 article that the treatment "does not make specific predictions about the heuristics that will be used in particular circumstances", and that it excludes anchoring. The confidence measure in the substitution-sensitivity studies is self-reported, and the replication's authors note that it may register the arithmetic difficulty of the problem rather than any sense of having answered a different question.
misreadings: The first error is quoting attribute substitution as a demonstrated process. It is a definition offered three decades after most of the studies it reinterprets, and Kahneman presents the 0.98 and 0.99 correlations as being in accord with it rather than as tests it could have failed. The second is the claim that the judge never notices. Kahneman wrote that the judge is normally unaware of the substitution, and De Neys and colleagues found that confidence falls when people substitute, from 95.60% to 84.95% in the McGill replication, so the unawareness is partial. The third is treating the Cognitive Reflection Test as a measure of substitution. Frederick introduced it as a measure of the disposition to resist the answer that comes first to mind, and whether it measures anything beyond arithmetic is disputed. Attali and Bar-Hillel gave CRT items to 252 people and then 567, alongside ordinary examination maths items with and without a tempting fast wrong answer, and report that a one-factor model fitted as well as any two-factor model, the CRT and maths factors correlating .900. Meyer, Attali, Bar-Hillel, Frederick and Kahneman answer on 4,407 people that a two-factor model fits better, cutting the RMSEA from 0.064 to 0.050, and that an eight-item reflection scale with no arithmetic in it correlates with the CRT at a disattenuated .88. The fourth is assuming every heuristic reduces to substitution. Kahneman leaves anchoring out. Oppenheimer reports across three experiments that people stop using availability to judge frequency once a salient cause for the ease of retrieval is available, so the swap can switch itself off. Shah and Oppenheimer propose a rival general account in which heuristics are sorted by the kind of effort they save rather than by what is substituted for what.
